summary.text: Paleoclimatology is the scientific study of climates from before weather instruments were invented, when no direct measurements were being taken.
Instrument records cover only a tiny part of Earth's history, so rebuilding ancient climate helps explain natural variation and how today's climate came about.
It reads proxies kept in rocks, sediments, ice sheets, tree rings, corals, shells and microfossils, and dates them to work out past states of the atmosphere.

items.prompt: Scientists can measure what Earth's air was made of hundreds of thousands of years ago. Where do they find samples of it?

items.prompt: A researcher wants to know a valley's climate 10,000 years ago. Why are recorded weather data no help?

options.label: The records were all lost in fires

items.explain: Climate data were only recorded from the mid-1800s, about 150 years, far too short to reach 10,000 years back.

items.prompt: Water with heavier oxygen-18 evaporates more readily when it is warmer. If an ice layer holds more O-18 relative to O-16, what does that point to, all else equal?

options.label: Colder temperatures when it formed
Warmer temperatures when it formed
A volcanic eruption that year
No change in temperature at all

items.explain: The ratio of O-18 to O-16 rises as temperature increases, though salinity and the amount of water locked in ice sheets also affect it.

items.prompt: Why do climate clues from very old sediments tend to be less reliable than younger ones?

options.label: Ancient climates changed too quickly to record
Older layers were laid down without minerals
Millions of years of pressure and fluids alter them
Scientists study them with older equipment

items.explain: Older sediments are more prone to diagenesis from pressure, tectonic activity and fluid flow, which lowers data quality and confidence.

items.prompt: Ice cores show distinct layers left by seasonal pauses in snow build-up. What are these layers mainly used for?

options.label: Linking each depth to a span of time
Measuring Earth's magnetic field
Spotting ancient meteorite strikes
Tracing the paths of ocean currents

items.explain: The layers can be used to build a chronology, tying specific depths of the core to ranges of time.

paragraphs.heading: Climate before thermometers
paragraphs.text: Paleoclimatology, spelled palaeoclimatology in Britain, is the science of climates from before weather instruments existed, when nobody could measure the weather directly. Instrument records cover only a tiny slice of Earth's history. Rebuilding ancient climates helps scientists understand natural swings and how today's climate came to be, and it matters for thinking about Earth's climate future too.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the clues
paragraphs.text: The field draws on methods from the earth and life sciences that recover information stored long ago in ice sheets, rocks, boreholes, sediments, corals, tree rings, shells and microfossils. These stored clues are called proxies. Once the proxies are dated, the records reveal what Earth's atmosphere was like in the past. Which method fits depends on what is being rebuilt, such as temperature or rainfall, and on how far back the climate in question lies.

paragraphs.heading: Early ideas
paragraphs.text: The notion that climate can change probably arose in ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley and China, which lived through long droughts and floods. In the 1600s Robert Hooke argued that giant turtle fossils found in Dorset meant the climate there was once warmer, and he thought a shift in Earth's axis might explain it. At the time, fossils were often put down to a biblical flood. In the early 1800s the amateur astronomer Heinrich Schwabe began careful records of sunspots, which started a debate about how the Sun affects Earth's climate.

paragraphs.heading: Becoming one science
paragraphs.text: Only in the 20th century did paleoclimatology become a single, unified field; before that, many separate disciplines studied pieces of climate history. Toward the end of that century, evidence about ancient climates began to be combined with ever more complex computer models. A new goal also appeared: finding past climates that resemble today's to learn about current climate change. Researchers study events such as Earth's many ice ages, sudden coolings like the Younger Dryas, and the rapid warming of the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum.

paragraphs.heading: Why older records fade
paragraphs.text: Weather records only began in the mid-1800s, giving about 150 years of data, which is no help for mapping a climate 10,000 years ago. Deeper time brings its own limits. The deep-sea record, which supplies most isotope data, exists only on ocean plates that are eventually pushed down into the Earth, so the oldest remaining material is 200 million years old. Older sediments are also more likely to be spoiled by diagenesis, as millions of years of pressure, tectonic activity and flowing fluids work on the rock.

paragraphs.heading: Air trapped in ice
paragraphs.text: Mountain glaciers and polar ice sheets hold much of the evidence. Ice cores drilled in Greenland and Antarctica reach back several hundred thousand years, and more than 800,000 years in the EPICA project. As snow is squeezed into glacier ice under later snowfall, air gets sealed into tiny bubbles, letting scientists measure directly what the air held when that ice formed. Seasonal layers in the ice link each depth to a span of time, and changes in layer thickness reveal shifts in snowfall or temperature.

paragraphs.heading: Oxygen and pollen
paragraphs.text: Changes in the amount of oxygen-18 in ice layers, written δ¹⁸O, track changes in average ocean surface temperature. Water containing the heavier O-18 needs a higher temperature to evaporate than water with ordinary oxygen-16. So the ratio of O-18 to O-16 climbs with temperature, although salt levels and the amount of water locked in ice sheets also affect it. Pollen trapped in the cores shows which plants grew when each layer formed, and sorting it by shape gives a count for that layer.
